clue.text: It takes two short months to boil

parts.note: DEC is the short form of December
OCT is the short form of October

explanation.surface: Something that needs a couple of months to come to the boil.
explanation.walkthrough: The two months are given in their abbreviated forms, December then October; 'takes' just links wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To decoct is to extract the essence of something by simmering it in water, a kind of boiling down.

clue.text: Suit for a flashy customer

parts.note: a suit of playing cards, and also the sparkling gems a showy dresser wears

explanation.surface: Clothing to fit a showy dresser.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suit' suggests clothing; it is a card suit, whose name is also the jewels a flashy person would wear.
explanation.definitionFit: One of the four card suits shares its name with sparkling precious stones loved by showy people.

clue.text: Was corporal punishment once so stealthy ?

definitions.text: Was corporal punishment once so stealthy ?

parts.words: Was corporal punishment once so stealthy ?
parts.note: the cat-o'-nine-tails was a whip once used for flogging; asking if it was stealthy plays on the animal's quiet tread

explanation.surface: A question whether flogging used to be done on the quiet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the cat' was the cat-o'-nine-tails, a whip used for flogging sailors and prisoners; something resembling a cat moves softly and stealthily.
explanation.definitionFit: Moving like a feline means moving quietly and stealthily.

clue.text: Its people, wrote Brooke, are "urban, squat, and packed with guile"

definitions.text: Its people, wrote Brooke, are "urban, squat, and packed with guile"

parts.words: Its people, wrote Brooke, are "urban, squat, and packed with guile"
parts.note: a quotation from Rupert Brooke's poem The Old Vicarage, Grantchester, mocking the people of a nearby university town

explanation.surface: A literary quotation about an unflattering view of some townsfolk.
explanation.walkthrough: Rupert Brooke, writing from Berlin in 1912, praised the village of Grantchester and mocked the nearby university town, whose people 'rarely smile, Being urban, squat, and packed with guile'.
explanation.definitionFit: Brooke's poem says the people of this English university city are urban, squat and full of guile.

clue.text: Might one expect to find them at New College ?

definitions.text: Might one expect to find them at New College ?

parts.words: Might one expect to find them at New College ?
parts.note: read 'New College' not as the Oxford college but as any college, where the new arrivals are the first-year students

explanation.surface: A question about who you would meet at a particular Oxford college.
explanation.walkthrough: New College is a real Oxford college, which steers you to its members; but the clue means simply the new people at any college.
explanation.definitionFit: First-year university students are the newcomers to a college.

clue.text: Advice to give praise to the Sappers

parts.note: RE, the Royal Engineers, are nicknamed the Sappers
commendation is praise

explanation.surface: Guidance to award honour to the army engineers.
explanation.walkthrough: The Royal Engineers (RE) are the British Army's Sappers; 'give ... to' sets the praise beside them.
explanation.definitionFit: A suggestion about the best course to take is counsel offered to someone.

clue.text: Rulers unaffected by a set-back

indicators.note: a setback here is reading backwards, and a word unaffected by that reads the same both ways

parts.note: these definition words give the whole answer, and the answer is itself the palindrome: it reads the same from either end

explanation.surface: Monarchs who carry on undisturbed by misfortune.
explanation.walkthrough: 'set-back' looks like misfortune; it means turning the word backwards, which leaves this palindrome unchanged.
explanation.definitionFit: Kings of Persia and Iran held the title used for a monarch there.

clue.text: Mother has her fling in these clubs

parts.note: MA is a familiar word for mother
to shy is to fling or throw, so she shies means she has her fling

explanation.surface: A mother lets her hair down at the nightclubs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has her fling' sounds like a fling in the romantic sense; it is shying, throwing something. Mashies are old golf clubs, roughly a five iron.
explanation.definitionFit: An old-fashioned iron used in golf was called by this name.

clue.text: Low-down way to catch a girl

parts.note: a net is a means of catching
HER is a pronoun for a girl

explanation.surface: A dirty trick for winning a young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Low-down' looks like 'underhand', but means lower in position.
explanation.definitionFit: Something lower down lies beneath, as in the underworld or lower regions.

clue.text: But it doesn't hurt those of a grasping disposition

definitions.text: But it doesn't hurt those of a grasping disposition

parts.words: But it doesn't hurt those of a grasping disposition
parts.note: the saying that if you grasp a weed firmly it will not sting you, and grasping here means seizing hold, not greedy

explanation.surface: A remark that greedy people never feel the pain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'grasping' suggests greedy; it means gripping firmly. The proverb 'grasp the nettle' says a nettle grasped boldly does not sting.
explanation.definitionFit: A common weed with stinging hairs is said not to sting if seized firmly.

clue.text: I cut a moat badly, working mechanically

indicators.note: something done badly is botched, so these letters are rearranged into a new order

explanation.surface: A poor attempt at digging a moat, done without thought.
explanation.walkthrough: 'badly' rearranges I CUT A MOAT, nine letters, into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that works by itself like a machine, without conscious thought, operates on its own.

clue.text: Seats arranged to some advantage

definitions.note: a noun phrase: a benefit or useful quality

indicators.note: arranged means put in a different order, so the letters of seats are reordered

explanation.surface: Chairs set out so as to gain the best position.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arranged' reorders SEATS; the definition is 'some advantage', a benefit.
explanation.definitionFit: A useful quality or resource is a benefit to its owner.

clue.text: Circular letter from Athens

parts.note: not a round-robin mailing but a Greek letter that is round in shape, the small o

explanation.surface: A newsletter sent round from the Greek capital.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'circular letter' suggests correspondence sent to many; here it is a letter of the Greek alphabet shaped like a circle, 'little o'.
explanation.definitionFit: The fifteenth letter of the Greek alphabet is written as a round o.

clue.text: Shell perhaps off target by three quarters of a mile

parts.note: to miss is to be off target

indicators.note: the word mile has four letters, and three quarters of it means three of them, dropping one

parts.note: taken as written before trimming

explanation.surface: A shell landing wide of the mark by most of a mile.
explanation.walkthrough: 'three quarters of' drops the M from MILE, leaving ILE after MISS.
explanation.definitionFit: An artillery shell is one example of a projectile fired at a target.

clue.text: Having this is an awful experience

definitions.text: Having this is an awful experience

parts.words: Having this is an awful experience
parts.note: read 'awful' literally as full of awe, so the thing you have is fear or terror

explanation.surface: A comment that some feeling makes for a terrible time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'awful' normally means very bad; taken literally it means full of awe, so having this feeling is an 'awe-full' experience.
explanation.definitionFit: Great fear or apprehension is the feeling of awe that fills an awful experience.

clue.text: Is he practically useless, or a perfect saint after one leaves ?

parts.note: ideal means perfect
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A question whether someone is impractical or a true saint once he has gone.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer with one (I) taken out reads IDEAL ST, a perfect saint: so 'after one leaves' describes what remains when I is removed, and putting I back between gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A dreamer guided by high principles is often thought to be of little practical use.

clue.text: There's a corresponding drop here

parts.note: 'corresponding' means mail, correspondence, which is dropped through a slot in a door

explanation.surface: A matching fall at some spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'corresponding' reads as 'matching'; it is to do with correspondence, letters posted through a slot.
explanation.definitionFit: Mail is dropped through a slot in a front door or into a postbox.

clue.text: Nooks for Parliamentary holidays

definitions.meaning: small hollows or alcoves set back in a wall
the periods when Parliament is not sitting

explanation.surface: Quiet corners for MPs on their breaks.
explanation.definitionFit: Alcoves set into walls share a name with the breaks when a legislature stops sitting.

clue.text: Cutting both ways

parts.note: a blade sharpened on each side, and figuratively an argument that helps and harms alike

explanation.definitionFit: A blade with sharp edges on each side cuts in either direction; an argument like that works for and against.

clue.text: A bird, or a dog may

definitions.meaning: a small bird with a long, constantly bobbing tail
a happy dog swings its rear appendage from side to side

explanation.surface: A bird, or what a pleased dog does.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as WAG TAIL, the second reading is what a dog may do.
explanation.definitionFit: A small songbird is named for its bobbing tail; a dog may wag its tail when pleased.

clue.text: One article about another noble Scot

indicators.note: about means around, so one article is placed around the other

parts.note: THE, the definite article, is another article
AN is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A piece of writing about a Scottish nobleman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts THE round AN; both pieces are articles in the grammatical sense, not pieces of writing.
explanation.definitionFit: In medieval Scotland a thane was a lord holding land from the king, ranking with an earl's son.

clue.text: Musical direction of an Italian poet

parts.note: Dante Alighieri is the great Italian poet

explanation.surface: The tempo marking a famous Italian poet gave.
explanation.walkthrough: Dante wrote the Divine Comedy; 'of' joins definition and wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: An instruction in a score to play at a moderate walking pace.

clue.text: First class clue for " pals "

parts.note: the word slap written upward, as in a down entry, gives pals

explanation.surface: A top-quality hint for the word 'pals'.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer read as an instruction says write SLAP upwards; in a down clue that turns it into PALS, which is the clue's word.
explanation.definitionFit: A slap-up meal is lavish and excellent, of the best quality.

clue.text: He takes what's left

parts.note: not a scavenger of leftovers but a person who receives what has been bequeathed in a will

explanation.surface: Someone who scoops up the leftovers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'left' looks like leftovers; here it is what a dead person has left in their will.
explanation.definitionFit: A person named in a will inherits the property bequeathed to them.

clue.text: Colourful sort of notes

parts.note: shades of a colour, and also musical sounds of particular pitch

explanation.surface: A bright kind of written memo.
explanation.walkthrough: The word means both shades of colour and musical notes.
explanation.definitionFit: Shades of a colour and musical sounds of definite pitch share this name.

clue.text: There's a movement afoot to use this

definitions.text: There's a movement afoot to use this

parts.words: There's a movement afoot to use this
parts.note: 'afoot' is literal: the foot moves to work a pedal, as on an old sewing machine

explanation.surface: Talk of a campaign getting under way to adopt something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a movement afoot' sounds like a campaign starting; literally it is the foot moving up and down to drive a pedal lever.
explanation.definitionFit: A foot-operated lever drives machines such as old sewing machines, lathes and spinning wheels.

clue.text: Odd, finding a mountain back in the Gromboolian area

indicators.note: back means the mountain word is read backwards

parts.note: an alp is a high mountain
taken as written

explanation.surface: A strange find of a mountain lying behind a nonsense land.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns ALP into PLA, then IN follows. Edward Lear's poem The Dong with a Luminous Nose speaks of 'the great Gromboolian plain'; 'Odd' sets Lear's nonsense mood and joins the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Lear's nonsense poem names a flat open region of land as the great Gromboolian one.

clue.text: They move back and forth, blown in the wind

definitions.text: They move back and forth, blown in the wind

parts.words: They move back and forth, blown in the wind
parts.note: not leaves in a breeze but brass instruments whose slides go to and fro while the player blows, the wind being the wind section

explanation.surface: Things swaying to and fro in a gale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the wind' suggests weather; it is the band's wind section, and these brass instruments are played by pushing a slide back and forth.
explanation.definitionFit: Brass instruments with a sliding tube are blown and played by moving the slide in and out.

clue.text: Refined Warsaw newspaperman

parts.note: Warsaw is the capital of Poland, so Polish describes it
ED is short for editor, a newspaperman

explanation.surface: A cultivated journalist from the Polish capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Warsaw' gives POLISH (of Poland); ED, the editor, is the newspaperman.
explanation.definitionFit: Polished manners are elegant and cultivated, free of roughness.

clue.text: Result of overtaking ?

parts.note: not passing a car but taking too much, over-taking, which leaves a surplus

explanation.surface: A question about what happens after passing another car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'overtaking' suggests passing on the road; split it as over-taking, taking more than is needed.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking more than is wanted leaves a surplus beyond the proper amount.
